notes: Plan fixes: file-share-soft-delete-share-scope becomes file-share-undelete-snapshot-recovery, and arm-what-if-resource-mutation becomes arm-what-if-reference-expression-resolution, to test administrator behavior. In 3.2, encryption-at-host-guest-execution becomes encryption-at-host-temporary-disk-key-source; vm-resource-group-move-region-preserved becomes vm-resource-group-move-resource-id; vm-region-change-in-place becomes resource-mover-commit-source-vm-retention; vm-scale-set-metric-autoscale becomes vm-scale-set-scale-out-rule-or. These replacements remove a name giveaway, overlap with b1, a recurring distractor and a broad autoscale fact.

cards.statement: Azure Storage keeps a Standard general-purpose v2 account's type fixed after an administrator creates it.
cards.explanation: To move data from a Standard general-purpose v2 account to a premium block blob account, create a replacement account and copy the data.

cards.statement: By default, the Azure portal configures new storage accounts with TLS 1.2 as the minimum version.
cards.explanation: The Azure portal sets a new storage account's minimum TLS version to 1.2. This creation default depends on the deployment tool.
cards.volatilityNote: The numeric TLS minimum and the portal's creation default can change.

source.title: Enforce a minimum required version of Transport Layer Security (TLS) for requests to a storage account

cards.statement: A GRS account allows applications to read blobs from its secondary region before an account failover.
cards.explanation: With geo-redundant storage (GRS), applications gain access to the secondary region after failover. Read access before failover uses RA-GRS.
cards.misconception: Geo-replication makes the GRS secondary region available for application reads before failover.

cards.statement: An administrator rehydrates archived blobs to an online tier before changing an account's redundancy.
cards.explanation: Azure Storage requires archived blobs to return to hot, cool or cold storage before the account's redundancy configuration changes.

cards.statement: Azure Storage requires change feed on the source account before an administrator configures object replication.
cards.explanation: Azure Storage reads the source account's change feed to identify operations that object replication needs to copy.

cards.statement: An application can directly modify blobs in an object replication destination container while its rule is active.
cards.explanation: Azure Storage rejects client writes to a destination container with an active object replication rule. Disable that rule before writing to the container.
cards.misconception: An object replication destination stays available for independent client writes.

cards.statement: Azure Storage copies a source blob's snapshots to its destination during object replication.
cards.explanation: Object replication excludes blob snapshots. Snapshots created for a source blob remain outside the replication policy's copied data.
cards.misconception: Object replication copies blob snapshots along with the blob's data.

cards.statement: Azure Storage can authenticate to Azure Key Vault with a managed identity for same-tenant customer-managed keys.
cards.explanation: Grant the storage account's chosen managed identity permission to use the key. Azure Storage uses that identity when accessing the vault.

source.title: Customer-managed keys for Azure Storage encryption

cards.statement: An administrator can resume an interrupted AzCopy transfer using the job's retained plan file.
cards.explanation: AzCopy uses its saved plan when resuming a failed or canceled job. It retries transfers in that plan that the job has yet to complete.

source.title: Find errors and resume jobs by using log and plan files in AzCopy

cards.statement: Azure Storage Explorer rejects a folder upload into a target virtual directory that it needs to create.
cards.explanation: Azure Storage Explorer creates a missing target virtual directory during a folder upload, then places the selected folder's contents inside it.
cards.misconception: An administrator must create the target virtual directory before Storage Explorer uploads a folder into it.

source.title: Manage Azure Blob Storage resources with Storage Explorer

cards.statement: By default, azcopy sync compares content hashes when deciding whether to update a matching blob.
cards.explanation: AzCopy sync normally compares file names and last modified timestamps. Content-hash comparison is an explicit option.
cards.misconception: AzCopy sync selects updated files by comparing their contents by default.
cards.volatilityNote: The default comparison behavior of the AzCopy sync command can change.

source.title: Synchronize with Azure Blob storage by using AzCopy

cards.statement: Administrators can edit a file inside an Azure Files share snapshot after creating the snapshot.
cards.explanation: Azure Files share snapshots preserve captured data as read-only. To change a captured file, copy it into a writable share first.
cards.misconception: A share snapshot acts as a writable copy of the file share.

cards.statement: Azure Files can restore a deleted share's snapshots when an administrator undeletes that share.
cards.explanation: Undeleting a retained Azure file share restores its contents and the snapshots that existed when the share was deleted. The recovery operation brings the share back as a unit.

cards.statement: Azure Files supports NFS deployments on SSD (premium) file shares in storage accounts.
cards.explanation: Azure Files offers NFS shares on SSD media. An administrator provisioning an NFS share in a storage account selects an SSD (premium) file share.
cards.volatilityNote: NFS support across Azure Files media tiers may change.

cards.statement: Azure Files converts an existing HDD file share to SSD (premium) when an administrator changes its media tier.
cards.explanation: Moving between Azure Files media tiers requires a new share on the target media tier and a data copy. An existing share's media tier stays fixed.
cards.misconception: A file share's media tier changes in place like a blob's access tier.

cards.statement: An account's anonymous access restriction overrides a container's public setting on the Azure Blob Storage endpoint.
cards.explanation: For Blob service requests, an account's prohibition of anonymous access takes precedence over a container's public setting. The account setting closes anonymous access to such a container.

source.title: Remediate anonymous read access to blob data

cards.statement: Container soft delete recovers a blob an administrator deletes from a container that still exists.
cards.explanation: Container soft delete restores a deleted container and its contents. A blob deleted from an existing container needs blob-level protection, such as blob soft delete.
cards.misconception: Container soft delete protects individual deletions inside a surviving container.

cards.statement: Azure Storage automatically keeps prior block blob content when an administrator overwrites it with versioning enabled.
cards.explanation: With blob versioning enabled, overwriting a block blob moves its previous state into version history. An administrator can access that earlier version to recover the old content.

cards.statement: Administrators can enable blob versioning on storage accounts that use a hierarchical namespace.
cards.explanation: Azure Blob Storage currently excludes accounts with a hierarchical namespace from blob versioning. Administrators need another data-protection approach for those accounts.
cards.misconception: Hierarchical-namespace accounts offer the same blob versioning feature as flat-namespace accounts.
cards.volatilityNote: Hierarchical-namespace support for blob versioning may change.

cards.statement: A new Azure Blob Storage lifecycle rule can act on existing blobs that match its filters and age conditions.
cards.explanation: Azure Storage evaluates stored objects against lifecycle rules during policy runs. Blobs that predate a new rule can qualify for its actions when their properties meet its conditions.

cards.statement: Administrators can select archive as the default access tier for a general-purpose v2 storage account.
cards.explanation: A storage account's default blob tier is an online tier. Administrators assign archive to individual eligible blobs rather than to the account's default access tier.
cards.misconception: The account's default access tier accepts archive just like an online tier.

cards.statement: Azure Storage automatically changes an archived source blob to hot when copying it into a new blob for rehydration.
cards.explanation: Copy-based rehydration creates a separate blob in the selected online tier. Azure Storage leaves the source blob unchanged in archive.
cards.misconception: Copy-based rehydration changes the source blob's tier along with the new destination blob.

source.title: Blob rehydration from the archive tier

cards.statement: Azure Resource Manager checks parameter inputs against allowed values before it starts deploying resources.
cards.explanation: A value outside a parameter's allowed choices fails validation. Azure Resource Manager catches this invalid input before it starts resource deployment operations.

cards.statement: An administrator can directly override an ARM template variable through the deployment's parameter file.
cards.explanation: A parameter file supplies values for parameters declared in the template. Variable values come from the template's definitions and expressions.
cards.misconception: A deployment parameter file directly overrides template variables as well as parameters.

source.title: Create an ARM template parameter file

cards.statement: Bicep automatically infers a dependency from a symbolic reference to another deployed resource's runtime property.
cards.explanation: A symbolic resource reference creates an implicit dependency in Bicep. Azure Resource Manager uses that dependency to deploy the referenced resource first.

cards.statement: A Bicep existing declaration automatically redeploys the referenced resource during template deployment.
cards.explanation: Bicep's existing declaration references a resource that is already deployed. The declaration does not submit that resource for creation or update.
cards.misconception: Declaring an existing resource makes Bicep include it in the resources deployed again.

cards.statement: A Bicep module can deploy resources into a resource group different from its parent deployment's group.
cards.explanation: A module's explicit scope chooses its deployment target. An administrator sets that scope to the desired resource group when deploying from the parent Bicep file.

cards.statement: Azure Resource Manager masks a secure parameter's value inside an ordinary string deployment output.
cards.explanation: An ordinary string output exposes the secure parameter's value in deployment history. The parameter's secure type does not transfer protection to that output.
cards.misconception: A secure parameter keeps its value protected when an ordinary string output includes it.

source.title: Test cases for ARM templates: Outputs cannot include secrets

cards.statement: An incremental ARM deployment can reset omitted properties when Azure Resource Manager redeploys a resource.
cards.explanation: Incremental mode reapplies the resource configuration. An administrator includes intended nondefault properties to preserve them when redeploying the resource.

cards.statement: A what-if operation can resolve ARM reference expressions before comparing resource properties.
cards.explanation: What-if compares a deployed value with an unresolved reference expression. It can predict a modification even when deployment would leave that value unchanged.
cards.misconception: What-if evaluates reference expressions just as a deployment does, so a matching resolved value prevents a predicted change.
cards.volatilityNote: Future improvements to what-if expression evaluation could change this documented limitation.

cards.statement: An administrator chooses API versions directly on individual resource declarations in an ARM template.
cards.explanation: The API version belongs to the resource declaration. Resources in one template can use different versions appropriate to their resource types.

cards.statement: An ARM template exported from a resource group preserves its original deployment's authored expressions.
cards.explanation: Resource-group export builds a new template from current resource settings. It does not recover the original template's parameter expressions.
cards.misconception: Exporting a resource group recovers the original authored deployment template.

source.title: Export a template from existing Azure resources

cards.statement: az bicep decompile can produce a Bicep file that needs repairs before an administrator deploys it.
cards.explanation: JSON-to-Bicep conversion uses a best-effort mapping. An administrator resolves warnings or errors in the generated file before relying on it for deployment.

source.title: Decompile an ARM template to Bicep

cards.statement: Encryption at host uses customer-managed keys for a VM's temporary disk when its managed disks use those keys.
cards.explanation: Encryption at host protects temporary disks with platform-managed keys. Choosing customer-managed keys for managed disks leaves the temporary disk's key source unchanged.
cards.misconception: Customer-managed key selection for managed disks also governs the VM's temporary disk.

source.title: Enable encryption at host for disks in the Azure portal

cards.statement: A successful resize of a running Azure VM preserves the guest operating system's uptime.
cards.explanation: Resizing a running Azure VM restarts the guest operating system. Schedule the size change for a time when the workload can tolerate that interruption.
cards.misconception: Resizing a running VM changes its compute capacity while keeping the guest running.

source.title: Change the size of a virtual machine

cards.statement: Azure preserves the existing data on a managed data disk after an administrator detaches it from a VM.
cards.explanation: Detaching a managed data disk leaves the disk available as a storage resource. An administrator can reattach it to a VM to access its stored data.

source.title: Detach a data disk from a Linux VM

cards.statement: Azure automatically formats a new empty managed data disk when an administrator attaches it to a Linux VM.
cards.explanation: Attaching an empty data disk makes it available to the Linux guest. The administrator then partitions and formats the disk before using it for file storage.
cards.misconception: Attaching a new managed data disk also prepares its guest file system.

source.title: Attach a data disk to a Linux VM using the Azure portal

cards.statement: Moving an Azure VM to another resource group changes the resource ID used by management scripts.
cards.explanation: A VM's resource ID includes its resource group. After moving the VM, update management references that still contain the old resource ID.

source.title: Move resources to a new resource group or subscription

cards.statement: An administrator can move an Azure VM between subscriptions belonging to different Microsoft Entra tenants.
cards.explanation: Azure Resource Manager requires the source and destination subscriptions to belong to the same Microsoft Entra tenant for a resource move.
cards.misconception: An ordinary subscription move transfers a VM across Microsoft Entra tenant boundaries.

source.title: Move resources to a new resource group or subscription

cards.statement: Azure Resource Mover deletes the source VM when an administrator commits a move to another Azure region.
cards.explanation: Committing a VM's region move leaves the source VM available for optional deletion. The administrator decides whether to remove that source resource.
cards.misconception: Committing a region move includes deleting the original VM.

cards.statement: Azure can reboot VMs in the same availability set update domain together during planned platform maintenance.
cards.explanation: VMs sharing an update domain can face the same platform-maintenance reboot. Check domain placement when evaluating an availability set's redundancy.

cards.statement: Uniform scale set instances use the standard Azure VM APIs that administrators use for standalone VMs.
cards.explanation: Uniform orchestration uses scale-set-specific VM APIs to manage its instances. Standard standalone VM operations are a different API surface.
cards.misconception: Uniform scale set instances expose the same management API surface as standalone VMs.

source.title: Orchestration modes for Virtual Machine Scale Sets in Azure

cards.statement: Azure keeps a scale set's chosen orchestration mode fixed after an administrator creates the scale set.
cards.explanation: The orchestration mode is a creation-time choice. To use a different mode, create another scale set and move the workload.

source.title: Orchestration modes for Virtual Machine Scale Sets in Azure

cards.statement: Azure autoscale automatically combines a scale set's scale-out rule conditions using OR logic.
cards.explanation: A matching scale-out rule can trigger an increase in scale-set capacity. The configured capacity bounds and cooldown still govern the scaling action.
